item.title: Life as Project Management
item.description: It is 2026, and I am preparing to manage my personal life and my family the way one manages a project. Why project management? Perhaps because I am getting older, and increasingly feel that life is finite — that one’s energy declines with age. Many things, if not done now, become very hard to adjust later when the body grows frail. Recently, spending time with my parents and looking back at photos from a few years ago, I have felt ever more strongly the natural aging of the biological body and the passing of youth. Now at the age when one is supposed to stand on one’s own, the sense of time pressure grows stronger, and many of the major decisions in life need to be put on the agenda. The older generation often says that there are things one should do at certain ages. Although the things they name may not be exactly the right ones, what is governed by biological law cannot be moved by personal will — for example, having children, sleep, exercise, and lived experience.

item.title: Reflections on Learning AIDD
item.description: I have recently been learning about AIDD (AI-assisted drug design). To summarize the field in one sentence: it uses AI models to predict the utility of drug molecules. That utility can be binding to a target, changes in biomarkers after the drug is administered, or even improvement in the disease itself. The drug molecule can be a known molecule or one generated by an AI model. The essence of AI-assisted drug design is to find a functional relationship that describes the mapping between drug molecules and their utility, and then use that relationship to find better drug molecules.

item.title: Lessons from Two Novartis Oligonucleotide Failures
item.description: Novartis’ two recent Phase III failures of oligonucleotide drugs have broken my preconception about this class of therapeutics — that suppressing target expression will, with high probability, translate into clinical efficacy. This view is essentially a static worldview: it assumes that flipping a single switch is enough to reverse a disease outcome. In reality, however, outcomes are shaped dynamically. There may be an initial trigger or a dominant factor, but as the disease progresses, multiple forces and effects compete and interact with one another.
